translation: Perhaps because Miho and Satsuki meet frequently in their hometown, they have similar expressions and ways of speaking.
Especially the way they eat sweets is similar, both of them breaking off small pieces of the cookie with their manicured hands and bringing it to their mouths.
I try to remember if it was like that before, but my memory is vague.
I think that the small habits and gestures of the two when we met before may have already flowed away somewhere.
Miho is now married, has bought a second-hand detached house in her hometown, and often has friends gathering there.

Though there are times when I feel reluctant about going to my part-time job tomorrow, it's the only connection I have with the world outside the convenience store and provides a valuable opportunity to interact with "normal women in their thirties" who are my same age.
Therefore, I try as much as possible to respond to Miho's invitations.

Today, the members, including myself, Miho, Yukari who still has a small child, and Satsuki who is married but does not have a child yet, gathered at Miho's house for tea with cakes we all had brought.
It was then that I was able to become a part of the world for the first time.
Just now, I felt as if I was born.
On this day, I was truly born as a normal part of the world.
For the two weeks leading up to the opening, we paired up and practiced tirelessly, pretending to serve imaginary customers while interacting with staff.

Looking into the customer's eyes while bowing and smiling, putting sanitary products in a paper bag, separating hot items from cold ones when packing them, and sanitizing hands with alcohol when asked for fast food.

In order to get used to handling money, there was real cash in the register, but the receipt had "training" prominently printed on it, and the customer was a part-time colleague wearing the same uniform.
It felt somewhat like playing shop.
My younger sister, two years my junior, was a "normal" child unlike me but she didn't avoid me; instead, she rather admired me.
When my sister, unlike me, was being scolded by our mother for something ordinary, I approached my mother and asked, "Why are you angry?"
Whenever our mother's lectures ended due to my questions, my sister, perhaps feeling defended, would always say "Thank you" to me.
As a child, I wasn't very interested in sweets or toys, so I often gave them to my younger sister.
Therefore, my younger sister was always following me around.
"Dad likes yakitori, so let's grill and eat these today," I repeated clearly, wondering if she hadn't heard me well.
My mom was taken aback, and the other child's mother next to us looked surprised.
Her eyes, nostrils, and mouth all opened wide at once.
I almost laughed because he was making a strange face, but seeing him staring at my hands, I thought, "Right, one isn't enough.
"Should I get more?"
Glancing briefly at the sparrows walking in a line nearby, my mother seemed to finally come back to herself and desperately called out, "Keiko!" in a reproachful voice.
"Let's make a grave for the little bird and bury it.
See, everyone else is crying too.
It's lonely since our friend died, isn't it? "Poor thing, isn't it?"
"Why? Even though they're already dead.
At my question, my mother was at a loss for words.
She quickly put canned coffee, cigarettes, and a corn dog into a small bag.
Meanwhile, the man who had been jingling the coins in his pocket suddenly reached into his breast pocket as if he'd just remembered something.
From that gesture, I quickly inferred that he would be paying with electronic money.
"Welcome, good morning!"
She gives a slight bow and receives the canned coffee offered by the male customer.
"Ah, also one pack of number 5 cigarettes.
"Very well.
Quickly pulling out a pack of Marlboro Light Menthol and scanning it at the register.
"Please touch for age verification.
Seeing the man's gaze swiftly shift to the showcase filled with fast food as he touched the screen, I stopped moving my finger.
"I could ask, 'Would you like anything else? But if the customer seems to be undecided about buying something, I tend to give them space and wait.
Reacting to the faint sound of coins, I turned around and looked towards the cash register.
People who jingle coins in their hands or pockets are often those who are about to quickly buy a cigarette or a newspaper and return, so they are sensitive to the sound of money.
Sure enough, there was a man approaching the cash register with a can of coffee in one hand and the other hand tucked into his pocket.
Swiftly moving through the store, I slipped behind the cash register counter, standing inside waiting so as not to keep the customers waiting.
The convenience store is filled with sound.
The sound of a chime as a customer enters, and the voice of an idol promoting new products over the store's public address system.
The sound of scanning barcodes, amidst the clerk's calls.
The sound of items being placed in a basket, the crumpling of a bread bag, and the click of heels pacing around the store.
Everything mixes together to become the "sound of the convenience store," constantly reaching my eardrums.
